units.text: INT. HUSBAND - CONTINUOUS
You can forget. Men easily forget. And I forgive. That is how women help the world. I see that now.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: Deeply overcome by emotion , embraces her .
My wife! my wife!
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: To LORD GORING.
Arthur, it seems that I am always to be in your debt.
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Oh dear no, Robert. Your debt is to Lady Chiltern, not to me!
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: I owe you much. And now tell me what you were going to ask me just now as Lord Caversham came in.
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Robert, you are your sister’s guardian, and I want your consent to my marriage with her. That is all.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Oh, I am so glad! I am so glad!
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: Shakes hands with LORD GORING.
Thank you, Lady Chiltern.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: With a troubled look .
My sister to be your wife?
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Yes.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Speaking with great firmness .

Arthur, I am very sorry, but the thing is quite out of the question. I have to think of Mabel’s future happiness. And I don’t think her happiness would be safe in your hands. And I cannot have her sacrificed!
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Sacrificed!
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Yes, utterly sacrificed. Loveless marriages are horrible. But there is one thing worse than an absolutely loveless marriage. A marriage in which there is love, but on one side only; faith, but on one side only; devotion, but on one side only, and in which of the two hearts one is sure to be broken.
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: But I love Mabel. No other woman has any place in my life.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Robert, if they love each other, why should they not be married?
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: Arthur cannot bring Mabel the love that she deserves.
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: What reason have you for saying that?
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: After a pause .
Do you really require me to tell you?
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Certainly I do.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: As you choose. When I called on you yesterday evening I found Mrs. Cheveley concealed in your rooms. It was between ten and eleven o’clock at night. I do not wish to say anything more. Your relations with Mrs. Cheveley have, as I said to you last night, nothing whatsoever to do with me. I know you were engaged to be married to her once. The fascination she exercised over you then seems to have returned. You spoke to me last night of her as of a woman pure and stainless, a woman whom you respected and honoured. That may be so. But I cannot give my sister’s life into your hands. It would be wrong of me. It would be unjust, infamously unjust to her.
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: I have nothing more to say.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Robert, it was not Mrs. Cheveley whom Lord Goring expected last night.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: Not Mrs. Cheveley! Who was it then?
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Lady Chiltern!
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: It was your own wife. Robert, yesterday afternoon Lord Goring told me that if ever I was in trouble I could come to him for help, as he was our oldest and best friend. Later on, after that terrible scene in this room, I wrote to him telling him that I trusted him, that I had need of him, that I was coming to him for help and advice.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN takes the letter out of his pocket .

Yes, that letter. I didn’t go to Lord Goring’s, after all. I felt that it is from ourselves alone that help can come. Pride made me think that. Mrs. Cheveley went. She stole my letter and sent it anonymously to you this morning, that you should think . . . Oh! Robert, I cannot tell you what she wished you to think. . . .
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: What! Had I fallen so low in your eyes that you thought that even for a moment I could have doubted your goodness? Gertrude, Gertrude, you are to me the white image of all good things, and sin can never touch you. Arthur, you can go to Mabel, and you have my best wishes! Oh! stop a moment. There is no name at the beginning of this letter. The brilliant Mrs. Cheveley does not seem to have noticed that. There should be a name.
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Let me write yours. It is you I trust and need. You and none else.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: Well, really, Lady Chiltern, I think I should have back my own letter.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Smiling .
No; you shall have Mabel.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: Takes the letter and writes her husband’s name on it .
Well, I hope she hasn’t changed her mind. It’s nearly twenty minutes since I saw her last.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Enter MABEL CHILTERN and LORD CAVERSHAM.
Lord Goring, I think your father’s conversation much more improving than yours. I am only going to talk to Lord Caversham in the future, and always under the usual palm tree.
units.name: MABEL CHILTERN

units.text: Darling!
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Kisses her .
Considerably taken aback .
